intro:
Every part of a free-response question is worth one point, and the first word of the part, its task verb, says what earns it. Identify asks for a name; describe asks for what it is like; explain asks how or why, with the because; compare asks about both things; explain the degree asks you to state the degree first.

Here you answer one part at a time: read the verb and its demand, write your answer with a checklist that watches for the because, then see the rubric line and a full-credit answer, and pick which of two answers earns the point.
howItWorks:
Explore. Pick a question and a part. The checklist under your answer is a hint, never a score: it looks for a link word in an explain (because, so), both sides in a compare, a degree in an explain the degree, and a scale when the part asks for one. Then open the rubric line and the sample, and choose which of two answers earns the point.

Test yourself. Seeded drills: what each verb demands, which answer earns the point, and the missing link of an explain. Each wrong choice names the slip the exam readers report most often. The questions are original and short; on the exam each question has seven parts, A to G, one point each.

contexts.title: Where people live in Country A
contexts.scenario: Country A is an invented country. Most of its people live in the Capital Region, in the center, and along the South Coast. Few people live in the Northern Hills or the Southern Forest.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify one physical feature that could explain why few people live in the Northern Hills.
parts.rubric: Names a physical feature that limits settlement, such as steep slopes, thin or poor soil, or a cold climate.
parts.sample: Steep, rocky slopes.
parts.sampleWhy: Identify needs only the specific thing, and a short phrase naming a real limit on settlement earns the point.
parts.weakWhy: This names no feature. Identify needs few words, but they must name the thing: steep slopes, thin soil or a cold climate.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of population distribution in Country A.
parts.rubric: Describes where people are and are not: concentrated in the Capital Region and along the South Coast, sparse in the Northern Hills and the Southern Forest.
parts.sample: People are concentrated in the Capital Region in the center and along the South Coast, and the Northern Hills and the Southern Forest have very few people.
parts.sampleWhy: It gives the characteristics of the pattern: where people cluster and where the land is nearly empty.
parts.weakWhy: One word names the pattern but does not describe it. Readers give no credit for "clustered" alone: say where people cluster and where they do not.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain one reason why many people in Country A live along the South Coast.
parts.rubric: Explains how a coastal advantage draws people, with the link: ports or trade create jobs, so people move there for work.
parts.sample: The South Coast has ports, so trade and the jobs that come with it gather there, which draws people looking for work to live on the coast.
parts.sampleWhy: It names the factor (ports) and then the links: trade and jobs gather, so people move there.
parts.weak: The South Coast has ports and jobs.
parts.weakWhy: It names two factors but never says how they make people live there. Explain needs the link: so people move there for work.

chain.link: so trade and the jobs that come with it gather there
chain.effect: which draws people to live on the coast

wrong.text: so the South Coast is next to the sea
wrong.why: This only repeats where the coast is. It does not connect the ports to people living there.

wrong.text: so the Northern Hills are cold
wrong.why: This is about a different place. The chain must run from the ports to the people on the coast.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how the pattern in Country A looks different at the local scale than at the national scale.
parts.rubric: Explains that one national number (density) averages the provinces, so it hides the crowded Capital Region and the nearly empty Southern Forest that local data show.
parts.sample: At the national scale Country A has one population density, but at the local scale the Capital Region is crowded and the Southern Forest is almost empty, because the national number averages all the provinces together.
parts.sampleWhy: It names both scales and explains why they differ: the national number is an average that hides the local differences.
parts.weak: At the local scale it is different.
parts.weakWhy: It says the two scales differ but not how or why. Explain needs the reason: one national number averages the provinces and hides their differences.

chain.cause: Country A has one national population density
chain.link: because that number averages all the provinces together
chain.effect: it hides the crowded Capital Region and the empty Southern Forest

wrong.text: because the map of Country A is drawn at a large scale
wrong.why: Map scale (the ratio) does not change the numbers. The scale of analysis, the unit each value describes, is what changes.

wrong.text: because the Capital Region is the capital
wrong.why: This repeats a name. It does not say why the national number hides the differences.

contexts.title: Living below sea level
contexts.scenario: For centuries people in the Netherlands have built dikes and pumped water out of low, wet land to make polders: dry land for farms, towns and roads, much of it below sea level.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Define possibilism.
parts.rubric: Gives the meaning: the physical environment may set limits, but people can choose how to use it and can adapt to it or change it.
parts.sample: Possibilism is the idea that the physical environment sets some limits, but people can choose how to use it and can change it with their culture and technology.
parts.sampleWhy: It gives the meaning of the term in a full sentence: limits from nature, choices by people.
parts.weakWhy: This is an example of possibilism, not its meaning. Define asks what the term means.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain how building polders in the Netherlands is an example of possibilism.
parts.rubric: Explains that wet, low land limited use, but people chose to drain it with dikes and pumps, so they adapted the environment instead of being controlled by it.
parts.sample: Much of the land was too wet to farm, but the Dutch built dikes and pumps to drain it, so they turned it into farmland; people changed the environment instead of being limited by it.
parts.sampleWhy: It goes from the limit (wet land), through the human choice (dikes and pumps), to the outcome that shows possibilism.
parts.weak: The Netherlands is low and has polders.
parts.weakWhy: It states two facts but never connects them to possibilism. Explain needs the link: people chose to change a limiting environment.

chain.cause: Much of the land was too wet to farm
chain.link: but the Dutch built dikes and pumps to drain it
chain.effect: so people changed the environment instead of being limited by it

wrong.text: so the environment decided everything the Dutch could do
wrong.why: That is environmental determinism, the opposite idea. Polders show people choosing to change the land.

wrong.text: so the Netherlands is a small country
wrong.why: The size of the country does not connect wet land to the choice to drain it.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe one environmental effect of draining wetlands to make farmland.
parts.rubric: Describes an effect with its characteristics, such as the loss of wetland habitat for birds and fish, or drained peat soil drying out and sinking.
parts.sample: Drained peat soil dries out and shrinks, so the land slowly sinks, and the drained fields sit even lower below the sea over time.
parts.sampleWhy: It says what the effect is like: the soil shrinks and the land sinks lower over time.
parts.weakWhy: This names the effect but does not describe it. Describe asks what it is like: why the land sinks and what that means for the fields.

contexts.title: Births, deaths and the transition model
contexts.scenario: A country's crude birth rate is high and has changed little, while its crude death rate has fallen fast over the last thirty years. Use the demographic transition model, a model that describes how birth and death rates change as a country develops.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the stage of the demographic transition model these rates are consistent with.
parts.rubric: Identifies stage 2 (a high birth rate with a falling death rate).
parts.sample: Stage 2.
parts.sampleWhy: Identify needs only the answer: a high birth rate with a falling death rate is consistent with stage 2.
parts.weak: A stage of the demographic transition model.
parts.weakWhy: This restates the prompt. Identify still has to name the specific stage.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain why the crude death rate falls in stage 2 of the demographic transition model.
parts.rubric: Explains how a change such as clean water, more food or vaccines leads to fewer deaths from disease or hunger.
parts.sample: Clean water, a better food supply and vaccines become available, so fewer people die from disease and hunger, which lowers the crude death rate.
parts.sampleWhy: It names the changes and then the link: fewer deaths from disease and hunger, so the rate falls.
parts.weakWhy: This names a factor and stops. Explain needs how it lowers the death rate: fewer people die of disease.

chain.cause: Clean water, more food and vaccines become available
chain.link: so fewer people die from disease and hunger
chain.effect: which lowers the crude death rate

wrong.text: so women have more children
wrong.why: That is about births, not deaths. The chain must explain the fall in the death rate.

wrong.text: because the death rate is lower
wrong.why: This is circular: it uses the effect as its own cause.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Compare the crude birth rate and the total fertility rate as measures of fertility.
parts.rubric: Gives a difference stated about both: the crude birth rate counts births per 1,000 people in a year, whereas the total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.
parts.sample: Both measure how many children are born, but the crude birth rate counts births per 1,000 people in one year, whereas the total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.
parts.sampleWhy: It speaks of both measures in one comparison: what each counts and how they differ.
parts.weak: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.
parts.weakWhy: This defines one measure only. Compare needs both: say what the crude birth rate counts too, and how the two differ.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the demographic transition model can predict a country's future population.
parts.rubric: States a degree, then explains it: the model shows a common path from high to low birth and death rates, but it comes from European history and leaves out migration, conflict, disease and government policy.
parts.sample: To a moderate degree: the model shows a common path from high to low birth and death rates, so it suggests growth slows as a country develops, but it was built on European history and leaves out migration, war, disease and government policy.
parts.sampleWhy: It opens with the degree, then gives what the model does predict and what it cannot.
parts.weak: The model was built on European history and leaves out migration, war, disease and government policy.
parts.weakWhy: This is a good limitation, but the degree is never stated. Readers want it first: to a high, moderate or low degree.

chain.cause: The model was built on the history of European countries
chain.link: so it leaves out migration, war, disease and government policy
chain.effect: which limits how well it predicts any one country's future

wrong.text: so every country will reach stage 5 at the same time
wrong.why: The model does not say this, and countries move at very different speeds.

wrong.text: so it is the only model geographers use
wrong.why: This does not connect the model's origin to how well it predicts.

contexts.title: How culture spreads
contexts.scenario: Cultural traits such as languages, music and foods spread from place to place in different ways: by people moving, through networks of cities, and today through the internet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the type of diffusion in which a trend spreads from a large city to smaller cities while skipping the countryside between them.
parts.rubric: Identifies hierarchical diffusion.
parts.sample: Hierarchical diffusion.
parts.sampleWhy: Identify needs the specific type, and this is it: spreading down a hierarchy of cities.
parts.weakWhy: The prompt already says diffusion. Identify must name the type: hierarchical.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe how relocation diffusion spreads a language.
parts.rubric: Describes the process: speakers migrate and keep using the language, so it appears in a new, often distant place without spreading through the places in between.
parts.sample: Speakers of the language migrate to a new place and keep speaking it there, so the language appears in a new area, often far away, without spreading through the places in between.
parts.sampleWhy: It gives the characteristics of the process: who moves, what they carry and where the language ends up.
parts.weakWhy: This names the cause in one word. Describe asks what the process is like: speakers move and take the language with them.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain one way the internet has changed the diffusion of popular culture.
parts.rubric: Explains how the internet lets a trait reach people far apart at once, so it spreads widely and fast instead of moving from place to nearby place.
parts.sample: The internet lets videos and music reach people anywhere at the same moment, so a trend no longer has to spread from one place to the next, which lets it reach the whole world in days.
parts.sampleWhy: It names how the internet works, then the link (no need to spread place by place), then the effect.
parts.weak: The internet is used all over the world.
parts.weakWhy: This is a fact about the internet, but it never says how it changes the way popular culture spreads.

chain.cause: The internet lets videos reach people anywhere at the same moment
chain.link: so a trend no longer has to spread from one place to the next
chain.effect: which lets it reach the whole world in days

wrong.text: because popular culture is popular
wrong.why: This is circular and says nothing about the internet.

wrong.text: so people stop sharing music online
wrong.why: This contradicts the cause: the internet makes sharing easier, not rarer.

contexts.title: Lines drawn from outside
contexts.scenario: At the Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885, European powers set rules for claiming land in Africa, and many of the boundaries they drew later became the borders of independent states.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Define a superimposed boundary.
parts.rubric: Gives the meaning: a boundary drawn by an outside power over an area, without regard for the cultures of the people living there.
parts.sample: A superimposed boundary is a border drawn by an outside power over an area, without regard for the cultures of the people already living there.
parts.sampleWhy: It states the meaning: who drew it and what it ignored.
parts.weakWhy: This points to examples, not the meaning. Define asks what makes a boundary superimposed.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain how a superimposed boundary can lead to conflict within a state.
parts.rubric: Explains the link: the boundary can put rival groups in one state or split one group across states, so groups compete for power or seek to join their kin, which can lead to conflict.
parts.sample: A superimposed boundary can put rival ethnic groups inside one state and split another group between states, so the groups compete for power, which can lead to conflict.
parts.sampleWhy: It goes from the boundary, through who ends up together or apart, to the competition that leads to conflict.
parts.weakWhy: This names an outcome and stops. Explain needs how the boundary causes it.

chain.cause: The boundary was drawn without regard for the groups living there
chain.link: so rival groups end up in one state and one group is split across states
chain.effect: which can lead to competition for power and conflict

wrong.text: so the boundary follows a river
wrong.why: Following a river makes a physical boundary; it does not explain conflict between groups.

wrong.text: because every boundary causes conflict
wrong.why: This is absolute and false, and readers give no credit for claims like it.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Compare a unitary state and a federal state.
parts.rubric: Gives a difference stated about both: a unitary state keeps most power in the national government, whereas a federal state shares power with regional governments such as states or provinces.
parts.sample: Both have a national government, but a unitary state keeps most power at the national level, whereas a federal state shares power with regional governments such as states or provinces.
parts.sampleWhy: It speaks of both kinds of state in one comparison.
parts.weak: A federal state shares power with its states or provinces.
parts.weakWhy: This describes one kind of state only. Compare needs both: say where power sits in a unitary state too.

contexts.title: The Green Revolution in India
contexts.scenario: From the 1960s, farmers in parts of India, such as the state of Punjab, began growing new high-yield varieties of wheat and rice, with chemical fertilizer and irrigation. This was part of the Green Revolution.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify one technology of the Green Revolution.
parts.rubric: Identifies a Green Revolution technology: high-yield seed varieties, chemical fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation or farm machinery.
parts.sample: High-yield varieties of wheat and rice.
parts.sampleWhy: It names one specific technology of the Green Revolution.
parts.weakWhy: Too general: identify still names the thing, such as high-yield seeds, fertilizer or irrigation. (Genetically modified crops came later, in the late 1990s, and do not count.)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain one positive effect of the Green Revolution on food supply in India.
parts.rubric: Explains how higher yields from new seeds, fertilizer and irrigation raised grain output, so India needed fewer food imports and faced less risk of famine.
parts.sample: High-yield wheat and rice, grown with fertilizer and irrigation, produced much more grain on the same land, so India needed to import less food, which reduced the risk of famine.
parts.sampleWhy: It names the change, the link (more grain on the same land) and the effect on food supply.
parts.weakWhy: This names an outcome and stops. Explain needs how the Green Revolution produced it.

chain.cause: High-yield seeds, fertilizer and irrigation came into use
chain.link: so farms grew much more grain on the same land
chain.effect: which reduced India's need to import food

wrong.text: so farms switched to genetically modified crops
wrong.why: Genetically modified crops came in the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.

wrong.text: so India stopped growing rice
wrong.why: The reverse: rice was one of the main high-yield crops.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain one negative environmental effect of the Green Revolution in Punjab.
parts.rubric: Explains how a Green Revolution practice harmed the environment, such as heavy pumping for irrigation lowering the water table, or fertilizer running off into water.
parts.sample: Farmers pumped large amounts of groundwater to irrigate their crops, so the water table fell, which leaves less water for farms and towns in Punjab.
parts.sampleWhy: It names the practice (pumping groundwater), the link (the water table falls) and the harm.
parts.weakWhy: This names two things but not what happened to the environment or why. Explain needs the link from the practice to the harm.

chain.cause: Farmers pumped large amounts of groundwater for irrigation
chain.effect: which leaves less water for farms and towns

wrong.text: so rainfall in Punjab increased
wrong.why: Pumping groundwater does not make it rain. The chain is about the water underground.

wrong.text: because the Green Revolution happened
wrong.why: This is circular: it names the topic, not a step in the chain.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of land use that the von Thünen model predicts around a market town.
parts.rubric: Describes the rings in order: market gardening and dairy nearest the town, then forest, then grain, then ranching farthest away.
parts.sample: Land use forms rings around the town: market gardening and dairy closest, then forest for fuel and lumber, then grain farming, then ranching farthest out.
parts.sampleWhy: It gives the characteristics of the pattern: rings, and what each ring holds, in order from the town.
parts.weakWhy: This names the shape and stops. Describe asks what is in each ring and in what order.

contexts.title: Models of the city
contexts.scenario: In the 1920s and 1930s researchers drew models of how land use is arranged in cities of the United States. After 1945 many of those cities spread outward into low-density suburbs.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify one cause of suburban sprawl in the United States after 1945.
parts.rubric: Identifies a cause, such as wider car ownership, new highways, cheap mortgages or cheaper land at the edge of the city.
parts.sample: More families owned cars, and new highways reached the edge of the city.
parts.sampleWhy: It names a specific cause of sprawl.
parts.weakWhy: This restates what sprawl is. Identify must name a cause.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Compare the concentric zone model and the sector model of urban land use.
parts.rubric: Gives a similarity or difference about both: both grow out from a central business district, but the concentric zone model uses rings, whereas the sector model uses wedges along transport routes.
parts.sample: Both models grow outward from a central business district, but the concentric zone model arranges land uses in rings, whereas the sector model arranges them in wedges along transport routes.
parts.sampleWhy: It speaks of both models in one comparison: what they share and how they differ.
parts.weak: The sector model has wedges of land use along transport routes.
parts.weakWhy: This describes one model only. Compare needs both: say how the concentric zone model is arranged too.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how suburban sprawl can raise the cost of public services for a city.
parts.rubric: Explains the link: sprawl spreads people out at low density, so longer roads, pipes and routes serve fewer people, which raises the cost per person.
parts.sample: Sprawl spreads homes over a large area at low density, so the city must build and maintain longer roads, water pipes and bus routes for fewer people, which raises the cost of serving each household.
parts.sampleWhy: It goes from low density, through longer networks for fewer people, to the higher cost.
parts.weak: Sprawl covers a large area at low density.
parts.weakWhy: This describes sprawl but never says how it raises the cost of services. Explain needs that link.

chain.cause: Sprawl spreads homes over a large area at low density
chain.link: so the city needs longer roads, pipes and bus routes for fewer people
chain.effect: which raises the cost of serving each household

wrong.text: so the central business district gets taller
wrong.why: This is about the city center, not the cost of serving the suburbs.

wrong.text: because suburbs are expensive
wrong.why: This is too vague and nearly circular. Say what makes the services cost more.

contexts.title: Measuring development
contexts.scenario: Countries are often compared by their gross national income (GNI) per person and by the Human Development Index (HDI) of the UN Development Programme. Development models such as Rostow's stages of economic growth try to describe how countries develop.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Define the Human Development Index (HDI).
parts.rubric: Gives the meaning: a UN Development Programme index that combines health (life expectancy), education (schooling) and income (GNI per person) into one score.
parts.sample: The HDI is an index of the UN Development Programme that combines a country's health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per person) into one score.
parts.sampleWhy: It says what the index is made of: its three dimensions in one score.
parts.weak: A ranking of countries from most to least developed.
parts.weakWhy: This is what the index is used for, not what it is. Define gives its meaning: health, education and income combined.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain why GNI per person alone may not show how developed a country is.
parts.rubric: Explains the link: GNI per person is an average and leaves out health and education, so it can hide poverty or poor services.
parts.sample: GNI per person is an average, so a few very rich people can raise it while most people stay poor, which means the number can hide how most people live.
parts.sampleWhy: It names the weakness (an average), the link (a few rich people raise it) and what it hides.
parts.weak: GNI per person is an average.
parts.weakWhy: This names the weakness but never says how it hides the level of development. Explain needs that link.

chain.cause: GNI per person is an average
chain.link: so a few very rich people can raise it while most people stay poor
chain.effect: which can hide how most people live

wrong.text: so it counts every person's income exactly
wrong.why: An average does the opposite: it blends all incomes into one number.

wrong.text: because GNI is a United States measure
wrong.why: False: GNI is used for every country, by the World Bank among others.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which Rostow's stages of economic growth describe the development of countries today.
parts.rubric: States a degree, then explains it: the model assumes one path, taken by Western Europe and the United States, and ignores colonialism and a country's place in the world economy.
parts.sample: To a low degree: the model assumes every country follows the path Western Europe and the United States took, but it ignores colonialism and each country's place in the world economy, so many countries have not moved through the stages in order.
parts.sampleWhy: It opens with the degree, then explains it with the model's assumption and what it leaves out.
parts.weak: The model assumes every country follows the path Western Europe and the United States took, and it ignores colonialism.
parts.weakWhy: The reasoning is good, but the degree is never stated. Readers want it first: to a high, moderate or low degree.

chain.cause: The model assumes every country follows the path of Western Europe and the United States
chain.link: but it ignores colonialism and each country's place in the world economy
chain.effect: so it fits many countries today only poorly

wrong.text: so every country reaches high mass consumption within 50 years
wrong.why: The model makes no such promise, and the record does not show it.

wrong.text: because Rostow was an economist
wrong.why: Who made the model does not show how well it fits.
